title: How to Judge Salary: Hourly to Annual Conversion for a 38-Hour Week
description: Learn how to judge salary offers by converting hourly rates to annual pay using a 38-hour week and 52-week year. Includes tax, super, and fortnightly comparisons.
salarySummary: Based on a 38-hour week and 52-week year, the national minimum wage of $26.44 per hour equates to an annual salary of $52,254.80 before tax and super.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect my annual salary estimate?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. When you use the timesheet, tick the casual loading checkbox and it will add 25% to your base rate before calculating the annual figure. For example, the national minimum wage of $26.44 per hour becomes $33.05 per hour casual, giving an annual estimate of $65,318.50 before tax and super. Remember, super is still paid on top of the casual rate.

faqs.q: How do I work out my fortnightly pay from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by 38 hours to get your weekly pay, then double that for a fortnight. For a full-time employee on the national minimum wage of $26.44 per hour, weekly pay is $1,004.90, so fortnightly pay is $2,009.80 before tax and super. Casual employees receive the same calculation but with the 25% loading, so their fortnightly pay would be $2,512.20. The timesheet shows both weekly and fortnightly figures automatically.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage ($26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026) is the legal minimum for employees not covered by an award or enterprise agreement. Award rates are higher minimums set for specific industries and occupations, found in pay guides from the Fair Work Ombudsman. For example, the Social, Community, Home Care and Disability Services Industry Award has its own pay rates. Always check the relevant award for your job, as award rates often exceed the national minimum. The timesheet uses the base rate you enter; you should verify that rate against the applicable award.

bodyMarkdown:
## Introduction

When you receive a job offer or are negotiating a pay rise, you need to **judge salary** offers fairly. Whether you are paid by the hour or on a salary, understanding how your hourly rate translates into annual, fortnightly, and weekly pay is essential. This guide explains the standard conversion using a 38-hour week and a 52-week year, and covers the National Minimum Wage, award rates, casual loading, superannuation, and tax.

## The 38-Hour Week and 52-Week Year

Australian full-time employees are typically expected to work 38 ordinary hours per week. This is the standard used by the Fair Work Ombudsman and the Fair Work Commission when setting minimum wages. The national minimum wage of $26.44 per hour is based on a 38-hour week, giving a weekly wage of $1,004.90.

When converting hourly to annual, we multiply by 52 weeks. This assumes you work every week of the year with no unpaid leave. For part-time or casual employees, the actual hours may vary, but the formula remains the same: annual gross ≈ hourly rate × hours per week × 52.

## From Hourly to Annual: The Formula

The basic calculation is straightforward:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For a full-time employee on the national minimum wage:
$26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,254.80 per year

This is your gross annual salary before tax and super. The same formula applies to any hourly rate. If you are offered a salary, you can reverse the calculation to find the equivalent hourly rate: divide the annual salary by 52, then by 38.

### Fortnightly Pay

Many employers pay fortnightly. To find your fortnightly pay, simply double your weekly pay. Using the national minimum wage:

- Weekly: $1,004.90
- Fortnightly: $2,009.80

For casual employees with the 25% loading ($33.05 per hour), the fortnightly figure is $2,512.20. The [timesheet](/) shows both weekly and fortnightly amounts automatically.

## National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage is the legal floor for employees not covered by an award or enterprise agreement. However, most industries have specific awards that set higher minimum rates. For example, the Social, Community, Home Care and Disability Services Industry Award has its own pay rates, and from 1 December 2026 home care disability employees will receive an initial increase of up to 15%.

To **judge salary** offers accurately, you must check the correct award for your job. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides [pay guides](/blog) for each award, listing minimum pay rates, allowances, and penalty rates. Always use the award rate that applies to you, not the national minimum, if you are covered by an award.

## Casual Loading

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave (sick leave, annual leave). The loading is added to the minimum rate, not included in it. For example:

- Base rate: $26.44 per hour
- Casual rate: $26.44 × 1.25 = $33.05 per hour

When using the [timesheet](/), tick the casual loading checkbox and enter your base hourly rate. The calculator will add the 25% loading before computing annual, weekly, and fortnightly figures. Do not enter a rate that already includes casual loading.

## Superannuation Paid on Top

Superannuation is paid by your employer on top of your gross pay. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to a maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. Super is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional contribution to your super fund.

For an employee earning $52,254.80 per year, the employer would contribute an extra $6,270.58 in super (12% of $52,254.80). This is separate from your take-home pay. The [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page explains more about salary packaging and super caps.

## Tax and Take-Home Pay

Your gross annual salary is subject to income tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% on excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: 30% on excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: 37% on excess over $135,000
- $190,001+: 45% on excess over $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (with reductions for low-income earners). The [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator on this site estimates your net pay after tax and Medicare, using the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds as the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed.

For the national minimum wage earner ($52,254.80), the tax would be approximately:
- Tax on first $18,200: $0
- Tax on $18,201 to $45,000 ($26,800): 15% = $4,020
- Tax on $45,001 to $52,254.80 ($7,254.80): 30% = $2,176.44
- Total tax: $6,196.44
- Medicare levy (2% of $52,254.80): $1,045.10
- Net pay: $52,254.80 – $6,196.44 – $1,045.10 = $45,013.26

This is an estimate only. Your actual tax may vary due to deductions, offsets, or the Medicare levy surcharge.

## Using the Timesheet to Judge Salary

The [timesheet](/) on this site lets you enter your hourly rate and choose whether you are casual. It then calculates:

- Weekly pay (hourly rate × 38)
- Fortnightly pay (weekly × 2)
- Annual gross pay (weekly × 52)
- Estimated tax and Medicare
- Estimated super (12% on top)
- Estimated take-home pay

This tool helps you **judge salary** offers quickly. For example, if you are offered a salary of $60,000 per year, you can enter the equivalent hourly rate ($60,000 ÷ 52 ÷ 38 ≈ $30.36 per hour) and see the fortnightly and weekly figures. You can also compare with award rates from the [pay guides](/blog) to ensure the offer meets minimum standards.

Remember that the calculator assumes a consistent 38-hour week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. It does not account for salary sacrifice, HELP repayments, or the Medicare levy surcharge. Always verify with your employer or a qualified professional for your specific circumstances.

## Conclusion

Converting hourly to annual pay using a 38-hour week and 52-week year gives you a solid basis to **judge salary** offers. Understand the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates, factor in casual loading if applicable, and remember that super is paid on top. Use the [timesheet](/) and [reference tables](/data) to explore different scenarios. For precise pay rates, always refer to the Fair Work Ombudsman’s pay guides and the Fair Work Commission’s annual wage review decisions.
